claims.text: The as-cast Nb–Ti–V–Zr–Hf alloy has maximal atomic disorder.
High chemical disorder creates local fluctuations in electron-phonon coupling.
Local fluctuations in electron-phonon coupling produce regions with enhanced pairing potential.
The locally enhanced pairing regions created by disorder are essential for superconductivity in this alloy.
Thermal annealing between 600°C and 900°C will reduce chemical disorder and promote atomic ordering.
Reduced chemical disorder will homogenize the local atomic environment.
Homogenization will diminish regions of locally enhanced electron-phonon coupling.
Diminishing the locally enhanced coupling regions will lower or eliminate the superconducting transition.
The as-cast samples are expected to exhibit a measurable superconducting transition down to approximately 1 K.
Annealed samples with reduced disorder are expected to have a lower Tc or no superconductivity relative to the as-cast samples.
Increasing annealing and atomic order should produce a systematic decrease in Tc.
XRD line broadening can quantify the degree of chemical disorder in these samples.
TEM atomic mapping can quantify local chemical order in these samples.
SEM/EDS can be used to rule out annealing-induced secondary phases or unwanted compositional changes.
The proposed relationship is limited to annealing conditions under which the alloy remains single-phase and retains microstructural integrity.
Stress relief or minor compositional changes during annealing could also affect superconductivity.
A verified reduction in disorder without secondary-phase formation, followed by no systematic decrease in Tc or change in transition sharpness, would falsify the proposed disorder-mediated mechanism.
